analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare hospitals and surgical centers to publish their prices, with penalties for noncompliance.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up: with no cosponsors, it sat in two House committees and their health subcommittees until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require Medicare hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers to publish a list of their prices — the full sticker price and the discounted cash price — for at least 300 common, shoppable services, in a consumer-friendly format. Hospitals with online price-estimator tools that meet federal standards would be treated as compliant. Facilities that refuse to post prices would face civil fines, and the government would publish each facility's compliance record. Hospitals would have to comply starting January 1, 2026, and surgical centers by 2028.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay cash, people with high-deductible plans, and anyone trying to compare prices before scheduling a non-emergency procedure. Published prices also give employers, unions, and insurers leverage when negotiating rates with hospitals.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers would have to make public, free of charge, their gross charges and discounted cash prices for at least 300 services patients can shop for in advance.

Facilities that fail to post prices after notice and a 90-day correction window would face daily civil monetary penalties — up to $2 million per year for larger hospitals and $300 per day for hospitals with 30 or fewer beds.
The Secretary would publish each facility's compliance status and enforcement actions on a public website, and flag noncompliant hospitals on the Hospital Compare site.
Hospitals could satisfy the shoppable-services requirement by maintaining an online price-estimator tool that gives an estimate without requiring an account or personal information.
The bill appropriates $10 million for fiscal year 2024 to implement and monitor the requirements, with a report to Congress on how the money was spent.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and ambulatory surgical centers bear the cost of compiling and publishing prices and the risk of fines for noncompliance. Some of that cost could pass through to what facilities charge, though transparency also pressures prices downward.

drawbacks.text: The requirements would fall on all Medicare-participating facilities, including small and rural hospitals; the bill responds by letting the Secretary waive or reduce penalties where they would cause significant hardship, such as rural areas where a penalty could reduce access to care.

Publishing sticker prices and cash prices does not itself force any facility to lower what it charges; the benefit depends on patients actually comparing and on insurers and employers using the published rates in negotiations. Federal hospital transparency rules already on the books require similar disclosures, and their enforcement has been widely reported as spotty.
The compliance deadline for hospitals is January 1, 2026 and for surgical centers January 1, 2028, so even had it passed, most of the benefit would have arrived years later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but indirect: shoppers can compare prices, and published rates give insurers and employers ammunition in negotiations. The costs fall on facilities, and compliance work is not trivial, though the bill phases in deadlines, accepts existing estimator tools as compliance, and gives small and rural hospitals a hardship waiver. The main weakness is that transparency alone does not cap prices — it only makes them visible.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees, then twice to a health subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Michelle Steel introduced the bill on July 24, 2023.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee.
The Ways and Means health subcommittee received the referral on July 28, 2023, and the Energy and Commerce health subcommittee received it on December 17, 2024; no further action was taken.
No member signed on as a cosponsor during the entire Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and surgical centers benefit from the bill's death: they avoid publishing detailed cash prices and face no new penalties or compliance costs. Patients are no better off through this bill, though the underlying policy goal is being pursued by existing federal rules.

for.name: Rep. Michelle Steel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on July 24, 2023.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its health subcommittee and took no further action; no markup or vote was scheduled.

against.what_they_did: Held the referral until December 17, 2024, when it went to the health subcommittee; no markup or vote was scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no roll-call votes, so no partisan pattern was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would force hospitals to publish sticker and cash prices for at least 300 shoppable services and exposes them to fines up to $2 million a year for noncompliance. Hospital pricing is opaque today, which lets facilities charge uninsured and cash-pay patients far more than insurers pay; public prices erode that advantage. The bill's deemed-compliance route through hospital-run price-estimator tools also leaves hospitals in control of how the information is presented.
The same disclosure requirements and daily penalties would reach surgical centers starting in 2028, including publishing cash prices or, where none exist, their median price over three years.
Facilities can comply by maintaining a qualifying online price-estimator tool, creating demand for vendors that build and run such tools on hospitals' websites.
